slides.title: Introduction to Economics
content: • Economics is derived from the ancient Greek word 'oikonomia'
• Means 'management of a family or household'
• Economics is a branch of the social sciences

slides.title: Definition of Economics
content: • Economics studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources
• Aims to attain the maximum fulfillment of unlimited human needs
• Studies how people choose to use scarce productive resources
• Resources include: land, labour, equipment, technical knowledge

slides.title: Key Aspects of Economics Definition
content: 3. Allocation of resources should be efficient
• Objective: Satisfy unlimited human needs through efficient resource allocation

slides.title: Nature of Economics
content: - Produces systematic, organized body of knowledge
- Facts are collected, classified, analyzed, interpreted

slides.title: Nature of Economics (Continued)
content: - Provides techniques and methods for achieving something
- Examines nature and causes of economic problems
• Conclusion: Economics is BOTH a science and an art

slides.title: Branches of Economics
content: • Foundation of modern economics rests on two major branches:

slides.title: Microeconomics
content: • Studies economic behavior of individual decision-making units
• Examines interactions through markets and industries

slides.title: Fundamental Problem of Microeconomics
content: • Also known as the problem of price-determination
• Example: Price of Teff, Price of Orange, Income of Aberash

slides.title: Macroeconomics
content: • Studies the economy as a whole
• Examines aggregate behavior of all decision-making units

slides.title: Fundamental Problem of Macroeconomics
content: • Associated with full employment of economic resources
• Deals with determination of income and employment level
• Tools used: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
• Example: GDP of Ethiopia, General price level in Ethiopia
• Focuses on equilibrium income and employment at aggregate level

slides.title: Differences: Microeconomics vs Macroeconomics
content: | Scope | Individual units | Economy as a whole |
| Focus | Income, prices, outputs | National income, general price level |
| Central problem | Price determination & resource allocation | Income & employment determination |
| Main tools | Demand & supply of commodities | Aggregate demand & aggregate supply |
| Examples | Price of Teff, Income of person | GDP of Ethiopia, Inflation rate |

sections.section_title: Methods and Approaches of Studying Economics

slides.title: Methods of Studying Economics
content: • Economics aims to establish valid generalizations (theories)
• A theory is a simplified picture of reality
• Both methods used to build economic theories

slides.title: Deductive Method
content: • Reasoning from certain principles to specific facts
• Enables arriving at particular conclusions from general statements
• Conclusions are then verified against observed facts
- Minor premise: Abebe is a man

slides.title: Inductive Method
content: • Proceeds from part to whole (particular to general)
• Develops theories based on observations and experiments
• Reduces the gulf between theory and practice
• Comprehensive data about economic conditions is collected
• Hypotheses are developed based on observations
• Example: Observing grain prices decrease during harvest → Generalization: increase in supply leads to fall in prices

slides.title: Positive Economics
content: • Describes the world as it is
• Answers questions: What is? What was? What will be?
• Does not judge as good or bad, better or worse
• Can be tested and verified with facts
- 'The number of secondary schools in Ethiopia is increasing'
- 'The current inflation rate in Ethiopia is 12 percent'

slides.title: Normative Economics
content: • Describes what the economy ought to be or should be
• Based on personal views about what is good and bad
• Cannot be proved or disproved with facts
- 'There should be government intervention in the economy'

slides.title: Decision Making Units of an Economy
content: • Economy is divided into different sections
• These sections are called decision-making units

slides.title: 1. Households
content: • Chief owners of factors of production:

slides.title: Households (Continued)
content: • Spend portion of income on goods and services
• Can be one person or multiple people living together
• May make joint or separate financial decisions

slides.title: 2. Business Firms
content: • Hire services of factors of production from households
• Sell to: households, other firms, government, or other countries
• Principal buyers of factors of production
• Consist of both private and government enterprises

slides.title: 3. Government
content: • Purchases goods and services from producers

slides.title: Government (Continued)
content: - Direct taxes: levied on households and firms
- Indirect taxes: levied on goods and services
• Uses commodities and factor services to meet collective needs
• Aims to satisfy combined needs of the people

presentation_slides.unit_title: The Basic Economic Problems and Economic Systems

sections.section_title: The Basic Economic Problems: Scarcity, Choice, and Opportunity Cost

slides.title: The Basic Economic Problem: Scarcity
content: • Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem
• All economic resources are finite/limited in supply
• Limited resources must be expressed in relation to unlimited human wants
• Scarcity reflects the imbalance between wants and means to satisfy them
• If resources were abundant, there would be no economic problems

slides.title: Scarcity vs Shortage
content: - Amount available is less than amount people wish to have at zero price
- People unable to get the amount they want at the prevailing price
• All shortages are a result of scarcity, but not all scarcity causes shortages

slides.title: Choice and Scarcity
content: • Scarcity → Limited resources → Limited output → Unlimited human wants
• Since output is limited, we cannot satisfy all wants
• Individuals, firms, and governments are forced to choose:

slides.title: Opportunity Cost
content: • In a world of scarcity, more of one thing means less of another
• The value of the next best alternative sacrificed is opportunity cost
• Definition: Amount or value of the next best alternative that must be sacrificed (forgone)
• Example: If resources can produce either 1 meter of cloth or 20 computers
- Opportunity cost of 1 meter of cloth = value of 20 computers

slides.title: Key Points about Opportunity Cost
content: • Measured in terms of goods and services, NOT money
• Based on the principle of substitution of one activity for another
• When opportunity cost increases, people substitute other activities
• Cost of producing a commodity is measured in terms of another commodity forgone

slides.title: Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
content: • Shows various possible combinations of goods and services society can produce
1. Quantity and quality of resources are fixed
2. Only two broad classes of output
3. Economy operating at full employment and full production
5. Some inputs are better adapted to production of one good (specialization)

slides.title: Alternative Production Possibilities
content: • Example: Economy produces Food and Computers

slides.title: Understanding the PPF Graph
content: • All points ON the curve: Attainable and efficient
• Points INSIDE the curve (e.g., Q): Attainable but inefficient
• Points OUTSIDE the curve (e.g., R): Unattainable
• The PPF describes three important concepts:
1. Scarcity: Cannot produce infinite output even with all resources
2. Choice: Movement along the curve denotes shift in preference
3. Opportunity Cost: Producing more of one good requires sacrificing another

slides.title: Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost
content: • States: As we produce more of a product, the opportunity cost per unit increases
• Makes the PPF concave to the origin
• Occurs because resources are not completely adaptable to alternative uses
• Formula: Opportunity Cost = Amount of next best alternative sacrificed / Amount of good gained

slides.title: Calculating Opportunity Cost
content: - Food decreases from 420 to 320 metric tons (sacrifice 100)
- Opportunity Cost = 100/500 = 0.2 metric tons of food per computer
• Taking absolute value: 0.2 metric tons of food per computer
• The economy gives up 0.2 metric tons of food for each additional computer

slides.title: Economic Growth and PPF
content: • Economic growth: Increase in total output level
• Occurs when one or both conditions happen:
1. Increase in quantity and quality of economic resources
• Represented by outward shift of the PPF
• Asymmetric growth: Growth in one sector only
- Shift of PPF along Y-axis or X-axis

slides.title: Basic Economic Questions
content: • Economic problems arise due to scarcity of resources
• Also called central problems of an economy
• Every modern society must answer three basic questions:
1. What goods and services are to be produced?
2. How to produce goods and services?
3. For whom goods and services are to be produced?

slides.title: 1. What to Produce?
content: • Also called the problem of allocation of resources
- Type of goods to be produced
- Quantity of goods to be produced

slides.title: 2. How to Produce?
content: • Also called the problem of choice of technique
• Once what to produce is decided, must choose production method
- Uses more labour relative to capital per unit of output
- Uses more capital relative to labour per unit of output

slides.title: 3. For Whom to Produce?
content: • Also called the problem of distribution of national product
• Relates to how material product is distributed among society members
- Produce for few rich people or majority of poor people?
- Focus on necessary goods or luxury goods?
• Many human efforts directed towards production to satisfy needs
• Economic activities occur within framework of economic system

slides.title: What is an Economic System?
content: • Set of organizational and institutional arrangements
• Established to answer basic economic questions
• Classified on basis of ownership of economic resources

slides.title: 1. Traditional Economy
content: • Relies on customs, history, and time-honored beliefs
• Depends on: agriculture, fishing, hunting, gathering
• Found in: Africa, Asia, Latin America, Middle East

slides.title: 2. Capitalist Economy (Capitalism)
content: • Production at initiative of private entrepreneurs
• Also called: Free market economy, Market economy, Laissez faire

slides.title: Features of Capitalism
content: 2. Freedom of Choice by Consumers (Consumer Sovereignty)
3. Competition among sellers, buyers, workers, employers

slides.title: 3. Command Economy (Socialism)
content: • Economic institutions owned and controlled by state
• Started in Russia (1917 Great October Revolution)
• Adopted by: China, Vietnam, Cuba, Ethiopia, etc.
• Lost acceptance after Second World War

slides.title: Features of Command Economy
content: 1. Collective Ownership (no right to private property)
- No private property means no profit motive

slides.title: 4. Mixed Economy
content: • Mix of private and public ownership
• Allows private and public sectors to co-exist

slides.title: Features of Mixed Economy
content: 1. Co-existence of Public and Private Sectors
- Public: Heavy industry, defense, power generation
- Private property allowed but rules prevent concentration of wealth

sections.section_title: Types of Resources and Factor Payments

slides.title: Types of Resources
content: • Resources are inputs used in production
- Examples: air, sunshine, solar energy, mountain stream
- Price is the test of whether a resource is economic or free

slides.title: Economic (Scarce) Resources
content: - All types of human resources (manual, intellectual, skilled, specialized)
- Most natural resources (fertile land, minerals, clean water, forests, wild animals)
- All types of capital resources (machines, intermediate goods, infrastructure)

slides.title: Four Categories of Economic Resources
content: - Physical and mental efforts of human beings
- Manufactured inputs used to produce other goods

slides.title: Renewable Resources
content: • Resources that have potential to be replaced over time

slides.title: Non-Renewable Resources
content: • Resources whose stock or reserve is limited/fixed
• Available supply may be replenished through recycling

slides.title: Conservation of Natural Resources
content: • Conserve = not misusing, spoiling, or wasting
• Renewable resources can also be depleted if overused
• Pollution: Harmful chemicals and substances released into nature

slides.title: Conservation Methods: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
content: - Turn off lights to reduce fossil fuel use
- Plastic jugs, jars, paper, bags can be reused
- Reuse natural resource/product to make something new
- Examples: glass, plastics, paper, cardboard, aluminum, steel

slides.title: What is a Market?
content: • An institution where two parties can meet
• Facilitates exchange of goods and services

slides.title: Goods and Services Market
content: • Where households purchase consumable goods and services
• Where businesses sell their goods and services
• Includes: stores, Internet, places where consumer goods are exchanged
• Money flows from consumers to business firms

slides.title: Labour Market
content: • Viewed at both macroeconomic and microeconomic levels

slides.title: Financial Market
content: • Any place where financial assets are traded
• Examples: bond market, stock market, share market

slides.title: Circular Flow of Income
content: • Shows basic economic relationships in a market economy
• Overview of how households, businesses, and government interact
• Exchange of: goods and services, productive resources, money
• Income and expenditure move in a circular way

slides.title: Types of Flows
content: • Economic transactions generate two types of flows:
- Factor services from owners to producers
- Goods and services from producers to buyers
- Money income from factor services (rent, wages, interest)
- Money expenditures for purchase of goods and services
• Real flows and money flows are two sides of the same coin

slides.title: Two-Sector Circular Flow Model
content: • Only two sectors: household sector and business sector (firms)
- Households spend entire income on consumption
- No saving, no government, closed economy
• Inner circle: Real flow (factor services, goods/services)

slides.title: Three-Sector Circular Flow Model
content: • Economy has three sectors: households, firms, government
1. Government Revenue: Taxes from households and firms
• Savings flow to capital market and to firms for investment

sections.section_title: Land as an Economic Resource in Ethiopia

slides.title: Importance of Land in Ethiopia
content: • Agriculture is the backbone of Ethiopian economy
• Land is a very important economic resource
• In agriculture context: refers to areal extent and productivity
• Suitability due to good soil and suitable climate

slides.title: Soil Types in Ethiopian Highlands
content: - Well endowed with required minerals for crops
2. Brownish-to-grey and black soils with high clay content:

slides.title: Climatic Aspect and Land Potential
content: • Formation of different agro-ecological zones due to altitude
• Different agro-climate zones → growth of different crops
• Increases potential for production of exportable items

slides.title: Land Ownership History in Ethiopia
content: • Pre-1974: Feudal system with inequitable land holdings
- Controls all urban and rural land with natural resources
• Rural peasants and pastoralists: Guaranteed lifetime 'holding' right
- Has all rights except sale and mortgage

slides.title: Current Land Rights Issues in Ethiopia
content: • Urban residents: Right to land for residence on 99-year lease
• Redistribution of land is highly restricted
• Access to rural land is almost non-existent
• Successive proclamations have violated this protection

slides.title: What is Demand?
content: • A desire becomes demand only when backed by:
1. Ability to pay for the good desired
• Demand refers to an effective desire
• Demand is always stated relative to:

slides.title: Definition of Demand
content: - The amount of it that a consumer is willing to buy
- At a given moment of time
- The amount of commodity a consumer is willing and able to buy
- During a given period of time

slides.title: Law of Demand
content: • States: Ceteris paribus (other things remaining the same)
- Price of a commodity and quantity demanded are inversely related
• Higher the price → Lower the quantity demanded
• Lower the price → Higher the quantity demanded

slides.title: Demand Schedule
content: • Presents various quantities of a commodity demanded at different prices
• Shows relationship between price and quantity demanded

slides.title: Demand Curve
content: • A graphical representation of the demand schedule
• Shows relationship between different quantities demanded and prices
• Example: As price falls from Birr 5 to 1, quantity demanded rises from 5 to 13 kg

slides.title: Demand Function and Market Demand
content: - Qd = f(P) where Qd = quantity demanded, P = price
- Total demand for a given product
- Sum of all individual demand at each price
- Horizontal summation of individual demand curves
- As market demand increases, price increases

slides.title: Supply vs Stock
content: - STOCK: Total volume of a commodity produced less quantity already sold
- SUPPLY: Quantity which is actually brought to market
• Producers do not offer all stock for sale immediately
• Example: Agricultural products kept in cold storage for better prices
• Supply may be less than or equal to stock

slides.title: Definition of Supply
content: • Supply of a commodity: Various quantities producers are willing and able to offer
- Number of goods/services suppliers will produce and sell
- Changes as price changes influence actual supply

slides.title: Law of Supply
content: • Demonstrates quantities sold at a specific price
• Unlike demand, supply relationship shows an upward slope
• Law states: Ceteris paribus, direct/positive relationship between:
• Higher the price → Higher the quantity supplied
• Lower the price → Lower the quantity supplied

slides.title: Supply Schedule
content: • Shows different quantities offered for sale at different prices

slides.title: Supply Curve and Supply Function
content: - Slopes upward to the right (positive slope)
- Qs = f(P) where Qs = quantity supplied, P = price
- Total amount all producers are willing to sell
- Horizontal summation of individual supply curves

slides.title: Concept of Equilibrium
content: • Equilibrium refers to a state of balance
• Physical world: Opposing forces balanced → object stationary
- No forces acting to produce change in values
- Consumer: No intention to re-allocate income
- Firm: No tendency to change output level
• Market Mechanism: Tendency to move towards equilibrium
• Equilibrium may never be actually realized

slides.title: Market Equilibrium
content: - Quantity demanded of a commodity equals quantity supplied
• Balance between opposite forces of demand and supply
- Price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
- Amount of good bought and sold at equilibrium price
- Quantity supplied by sellers matches quantity demanded by buyers

slides.title: Graphical Representation of Market Equilibrium
content: • Demand curve and Supply curve intersect
- Quantity consumers want to purchase matches
- Changes over time due to shifts in demand/supply

sections.section_title: Definition of Production, Inputs and Outputs

slides.title: What is Production?
content: • Production is a process of combining various inputs
• Aims to produce an output for consumption
• The act of creating output in form of commodity or service
• Contributes to the utility of individuals
• Example: Producing wheat using land, labour, capital, seeds

slides.title: Inputs and Outputs
content: • INPUTS: Economic resources used in production
• OUTPUTS: Inputs transformed into final usable form
- Give less satisfaction to consumer by themselves

slides.title: Tangible vs Intangible Outputs
content: - Physical products that can be touched
- Have value but not physical objects
- Cannot often be tried out, inspected, or tested in advance
- Examples: insurance, consultancy, software, education, healthcare

slides.title: Types of Inputs
content: - Quantity cannot be varied during the period
- Quantity can be changed during the period

slides.title: Short Run vs Long Run
content: • Based on degree of flexibility of economic resources
- At least one input is fixed
- Increase output by using more variable inputs
- Examples: Using more labour and raw materials
- All inputs are variable (no fixed input)
- Firm can change size of plant

slides.title: Important Note on Time Periods
content: • 'Short run' and 'long run' do NOT refer to specific time periods:
- Not: one year or less, two or five years
• Refers to nature of economic arrangement of inputs
• Based on response to changing economic environment
• Short run: Some factors can't be adjusted
• Long run: All factors can be adjusted

slides.title: Measures of Productivity
content: - Uses combination of variable inputs with fixed inputs
- Total output divided by number of workers employed
- Formula: AP = TP/L where L = Labour
- Good indicator of productivity of labour

slides.title: Marginal Product (MP)
content: - The increase in output from using one additional unit of a single factor
- Where ΔTP = change in total production
• TP, MP, and AP are interrelated

slides.title: Production Function with One Variable Input (Example)
content: | Labour | Capital | TP | AP | MP | Stage |

slides.title: Stages of Production
content: - MP is rising and greater than AP
- MP is falling but still positive

slides.title: What is Cost of Production?
content: • Concepts of production and cost are inseparable
- Monetary outlays associated with production activity
- In the entire process of production and distribution of goods and services

slides.title: Explicit and Implicit Costs
content: - Actual monetary payments made to outsiders
- Include: wages, rent, interest, payments for raw materials, fuel, transport
- Values of non-purchased resources owned and used by firms
- Examples: salary of owner-manager, estimated rent of owned building
- Estimated from what they could earn in best alternative uses

slides.title: Economic Cost vs Accounting Cost
content: - Includes both implicit and explicit costs
- Economic Cost = Implicit Costs + Explicit Costs
- Monetary value of all purchased inputs
- Includes: wages, cost of raw materials, depreciation, interest on borrowed funds, utility expenses

slides.title: Fixed and Variable Costs
content: - Costs that do not vary with output level
- Always incurred even if firm produces nothing
- Examples: rent on leased properties, interest on borrowed funds, wear and tear of machinery, cost of administrative staff
- Costs that directly vary with output level
- Examples: wages of workers (excluding admin staff), cost of raw materials

slides.title: Total Cost
content: • Total Cost (TC) = Total Fixed Cost (TFC) + Total Variable Cost (TVC)

slides.title: Cost Curves
content: • TFC: Parallel to quantity axis, constant at 60 birr
• TC: Sum of TVC and TFC at every output level
• TC curve has same shape as TVC
• Shape reflects law of diminishing returns

slides.title: Marginal Cost (MC)
content: - The additional total cost from producing one more unit of output
- Change in total cost from a unit change in output
- In short run: MC = ΔTVC/ΔQ (since ΔTFC = 0)
• Example: If TC increases from 260 to 293 when output increases from 50 to 51 units:

slides.title: What is Money?
content: • Definition: Anything generally accepted in payment for goods or services or in repayment of debts
• Any good widely used and accepted in transactions
• A commodity accepted by general consent as a medium of economic exchange
- Medium for expressing prices and values
- Circulates anonymously from person to person and country to country

slides.title: Key Characteristics of Money
content: • Immediately exchangeable for all kinds of marketable assets
• Each person accepts money because confident others will accept it
• Social convention through legal or other means

slides.title: Criteria for a Commodity to be Accepted as Money
content: - Widely accepted as a medium of exchange

slides.title: The Barter System
content: • Life among ancient humans was simple and self-sufficient
• Barter: Direct exchange of goods for goods
• Individual produces surplus to exchange for needed items
• Economy based on this system: Barter Economy
• Major limitations led to development of money

slides.title: Limitations of Barter System
content: 1. Lack of Double Coincidence of Wants:
- Need to find someone who wants what you have AND has what you want
2. Lack of Common Measure of Value:
- No standard to determine exchange ratios
4. Difficulty in Storing and Transferring Wealth:
- Many goods lose value over time or have high storage/transportation costs
- Price instability and lack of quality standards

slides.title: Evolution of Money Globally
content: • Barter → Commodity Money → Paper Currency → Fiat Money → Checks → Electronic Money
• Commodity Money: Precious metals or valuable items
- Problems: Heavy and hard to transport
• Paper Currency: Initially convertible into coins/precious metal
- Disadvantage: Trust required, difficult to counterfeit
• Fiat Money: Decreed by governments as legal tender
- Not convertible into coins or precious metal

slides.title: Checks and Electronic Money
content: - Transactions without carrying large amounts of currency
- Examples: visa cards, credit cards, etc.

slides.title: History of Money in Ethiopia
content: • After Axum's fall: Commodity money used
- Salt (amole) most important and widely spread
• National coins: Emperor Menelik II (1893), Emperor Haileselassie I (1933)

slides.title: History of Money in Ethiopia (Continued)
content: • First Paper Money: Bank of Abyssinia (1914)
• Bank of Ethiopia (1932): 100% backed by gold deposits
- East African Shilling, Indian Rupee, Egyptian Pound
• July 1945: Ethiopian government issued new national currency - BIRR
• With banking development: Checks started to be used

slides.title: Four Basic Functions of Money
content: In every society, money performs four basic functions:
All these functions play significant roles in the economy's operation

slides.title: 1. Medium of Exchange
content: • Used to pay for goods and services
• Used in almost all market transactions
• Money has no direct power to satisfy wants
- But has power to purchase things that satisfy wants
- Eliminates time spent exchanging goods (transaction cost)
• Lower transaction costs → encourage specialization and division of labour

slides.title: 2. Unit of Account (Measure of Value)
content: • Used to measure value in the economy
• Measures value of goods and services in terms of money
• Like measuring weight in pounds or distance in miles

slides.title: 3. Store of Value
content: • A repository of purchasing power over time
• Used to save purchasing power from when income is received until it is spent
• Useful because most people don't want to spend income immediately
• Money is not unique as a store of value
• Other assets (stocks, bonds, land, houses, art) can store wealth
• Many assets have advantages over money:

slides.title: Liquidity and Money
content: • Question: If other assets are better stores of value, why hold money?
• LIQUIDITY: The relative ease and speed with which an asset can be
converted to a medium of exchange
• Money is the most liquid asset
• Other assets must be converted to money before spending

slides.title: 4. Standard of Deferred Payments
content: • Allows buying now and paying later
• Allows lending now and collecting later
- Money can be borrowed and channeled into investments
• Permits transfer of spending power from:
• Allows easy transfer of resources from less desired uses
- To more desired uses (more productive, more profitable)

slides.title: Demand for Money (Liquidity Preference)
content: • Traditional View: Money demanded for completing business transactions
- Depends on volume of trade or transactions
• Modern View (Keynes): Demand for money to hold
• Three main reasons people want to hold money:

slides.title: 1. Transaction Motive
content: • Demand for money for current transactions
- To bridge interval between receipt of income and its expenditure
- Depends on: size of income, receipt interval, methods of payment
- Keep ready cash to meet current needs
- Pay for raw materials, transport, wages, salaries

slides.title: 2. Precautionary Motive
content: • Desire to hold cash balances for unforeseen contingencies

slides.title: 3. Speculative Motive
content: • Desire to hold resources in liquid form
• To take advantage of market movements
• Money held under this motive serves as a store of value
• Amount of money required under various motives constitutes demand for money

slides.title: Supply of Money
content: • Supply of money = Supply of money to hold
• Money must always be held by someone
• Definition: Sum total of all forms of money held by a community at any given moment
(b) Currency notes issued by currency authority

slides.title: Money Supply in a Country
content: • Total volume of monetary medium of exchange available to the community
• In developing countries: Currency dominates over bank deposits
• Supply depends on credit control policies of banking system
• National Bank of Ethiopia issues bulk of currency

slides.title: What is Electronic Money?
content: • Allows 24-hour access to cash through ATMs

slides.title: Advantages of E-money
content: 4. Ability to move large sums of money without physical burden

slides.title: Disadvantages of E-money
content: 2. New digital forms of money laundering
3. Users must have minimum level of training and knowledge
4. Some types (especially cryptocurrencies) linked to criminal activity
7. Not universally accepted in all locations

slides.title: What is Macroeconomics?
content: • Branch of economics dealing with economy as a whole
• Focuses on: performance, structure, behavior, decision-making
• Includes: regional, national, and global economies
• Uses interest rates, taxes, government spending to regulate growth and stability
• Topics studied: GDP, unemployment, national income, price indices, inflation, trade

slides.title: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
content: • Definition: Total value of currently produced final goods and services
- During a given period (usually one year)
2. Includes final goods and services only (end products)
- Qi = quantities of final goods and services

slides.title: Gross National Product (GNP)
content: • Definition: Total value of goods and services
- Produced by domestically owned factors of production
- During a given time period (usually one year)
- NFI = Net Factor Income from Foreign Sources
• NFI = (Factor income received from abroad) - (Factor income paid for foreigners abroad)

slides.title: Per Capita Income
content: • Definition: Ratio of GDP of a country to its total population
• Purpose: Determines average income of individual citizens
• Enables evaluation of living standard of the population
• Useful for comparing living standards between countries

slides.title: General Objectives of Macroeconomic Policy
content: Nations adopt macroeconomic policies to bring desirable changes in aggregate variables.
5. Fair Distribution of Income and Wealth
Policies vary according to economic conditions of specific economy

slides.title: Detailed Macroeconomic Goals
content: - Maximum possible utilization of factors of production
- Statistical record of economic transactions between residents and rest of world in equilibrium
- Stable level of prices avoiding inflation or deflation
- Sustains value of money over time
5. FAIR DISTRIBUTION OF INCOME AND WEALTH

slides.title: Macroeconomic Problems
content: • Economy does not always run smoothly
• Recession: Levels of national income, output, and employment

slides.title: 1. Inflation
content: • Definition: Sustained increase in the general price level
- Small rise in prices is not inflation
- Persistent and appreciable rise in prices
- All costs and prices do not rise together or in same proportion
- Measured by price index (average of consumer/producer prices)
• Economy can fluctuate between both conditions

slides.title: Causes and Types of Inflation
content: - Due to: bad weather, wage increases, input price increases

slides.title: 2. Unemployment
content: • Definition: Individuals who are employable, actively seeking a job, but unable to find one
- Population aged 15-64 who are fit, willing, and available to work
- Includes both employed and unemployed people
• For a person to be unemployed:
1. Must be without a job and able to work
2. Must want a job and willing to work at current market wage
• Unemployment Rate: (Number of unemployed / Total labor force) × 100

slides.title: Types of Unemployment
content: - Mismatch between skills/locations and job requirements/locations
- Due to changes in demand pattern or structure of production
- Associated with recession/depression period of trade cycle

slides.title: Disguised Unemployment in Ethiopian Economy
content: • Unemployment that does not affect aggregate economic output
- Too many workers filling too few jobs
- Workers are involved in redundant work
• Also called hidden unemployment or labor surplus

slides.title: 3. Trade Balance Deficit
content: • Trade Balance = Receipts for exported goods - Payments on imported goods
• SURPLUS: Country earned more from exports than paid for imports
• DEFICIT: Country paid more for imports than earned from exports
• Ethiopian economy has experienced deficit balance of trade:
- Export receipts fall short of import expenditure

slides.title: 4. Balance of Payments Deficit
content: • Balance of Payments: Statistical record of all economic transactions between
- Residents of the reporting country AND
- Residents of the rest of the world
- How many goods and services exported and imported
- Whether country borrowed from or lent to rest of world
- Changes in reserves of foreign currency
• DEFICIT: Total payments exceed total receipts

sections.section_title: Definition of Enterprise, Entrepreneur and Entrepreneurship

slides.title: Core Concepts
content: - Legal entity possessing right to conduct business
- Can enter into contracts, own property, incur liabilities, establish bank accounts
- Any person who creates and develops a business idea
- Takes risk of setting up enterprise
- Process of identifying opportunities in marketplace
- Investing resources to exploit opportunities for long term gains

slides.title: Key Aspects of Entrepreneurship
content: - Bringing together resources in new ways
• Critical in countries with high unemployment rates (like Ethiopia)
• Requires creativity as driving force behind innovation

slides.title: Abilities of an Entrepreneur
content: 1. Ability to spot a potentially profitable opportunity
2. Ability to commercialize the perceived opportunity (Innovation)
3. Ability to pursue it in the long term
5. Acceptance of failure as a possibility
• Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu: Founded SoleRebels (shoe company using recycled tires)
- Named fastest growing brand in Africa by Forbes
• Haile Gebrselassie: Retired athlete, owns Marathon Motors (assembles Hyundai vehicles)

slides.title: History of Entrepreneurship
content: - 'Entrepreneur' referred to person managing large commercial projects
- Person with contractual agreement with government
- To provide stipulated products or services
- Richard Cantillon: Entrepreneur is a risk-taker
- Differentiated entrepreneurial role from capital providing role

slides.title: History of Entrepreneurship (Continued)
content: - Organizes and operates enterprise for personal gain
- Concept of entrepreneur as an inventor established
- Application of innovation in business ideas

slides.title: Social Entrepreneurship
content: - Process by which individuals, start-ups, entrepreneurs
- Develop and find solutions that directly address social issues
- Interesting and appealing about entrepreneurs and their stories
- People like Muhammad Yunus and Steve Jobs are attracted
- Commanding role in driving social change
- Potential payoff with benefit to society

sections.section_title: Creativity and Innovation in Solving Local Problems

slides.title: Creativity, Innovation, and Entrepreneurship
content: • Recognized as important contributors to nation's economic growth
- Tendency to generate ideas, alternatives, or possibilities
- Useful in solving problems, communicating, entertaining
- Ability to come up with new ideas
- Identify new ways of looking at problems and opportunities
• Entrepreneurship: Exploitation of opportunities through creativity and innovation

slides.title: Key Elements of Creativity
content: Definition of Creativity has three key elements:
- Creative process of putting things together
To be creative: Need to view things in new ways from different perspectives

slides.title: Innovation
content: • Lies at the heart of the entrepreneurial process
• A means to the exploitation of opportunities
• Implementation of a new idea at:
1. INVENTION: Creation of a new product, service, or process
2. EXPANSION: Growth of a product, service, or process
3. DUPLICATION: Replication of an already existing product, service, or process
4. SYNTHESIS: Combination of existing concepts and factors into a new formulation

slides.title: From Creativity to Entrepreneurship
content: • CREATIVITY: Ability to develop new ideas and discover new ways
• INNOVATION: Ability to apply creative solutions
- Improve people's lives or enrich society
- Creativity leads to generation of novel business ways
- Exploring new niches and coming up with new ideas
- Leads to efficiency and competitive advantage
• Creative entrepreneurs are investors in talent:

slides.title: Entrepreneurial Mind-set
content: • A state of mind that an individual possesses
• The way people think and their attitude towards goals
• Important tool that enables entrepreneurial activities
• Their mind-set gives business the best chance of surviving
• Means they are brave in decisions they make
• Actively seek clients and take risks
• Not all entrepreneurs succeed: Successful entrepreneurs fail at least once
• Key: Learn from failures and exploit them

slides.title: Key Attitudes Every Entrepreneur Must Have
content: - Passionate about ideas, goals, and companies
- Fear of not succeeding doesn't stop them
- Use fear to push themselves harder

slides.title: Key Attitudes (Continued)
content: - Not easy to start from ground up
- Many hours of hard work, frustration, creativity, supervision
- Always working: establishing new ideas, creating new products, designing new processes, hiring clever people
- Colleagues, sellers, customers, investors must trust them
- Suppliers need to know payments arrive on time
- Customers need to know products/services delivered as promised

slides.title: Skills and Attributes to be More Innovative
content: • Entrepreneur: Has good business idea AND can turn it into reality
• Turning idea into reality based on two kinds of skills:

slides.title: General Management Skills
content: - Think about business as a whole
- Understand how it fits into market
- Organize to deliver value better than competitors
- Prepare for what needs to be done now

slides.title: General Management Skills (Continued)
content: - Ensure resources in right place at right time

slides.title: People Management Skills
content: - Inform others orally and in writing
- Inspire people to work in a certain way
- Entice and compel people to complete tasks
- Understand what people expect from jobs

slides.title: People Management Skills (Continued)
content: - Use skills to achieve future business needs
- Understand what is required in a situation
- Identify opportunities to maximize outcomes for all parties

slides.title: Identifying Entrepreneurial Opportunities
content: • Not every idea is necessarily a good one
• An idea becomes an opportunity when:
- Possibility of satisfying the requested product/service
• Criteria to move from idea to opportunity:

slides.title: How Opportunities are Found
content: - Making a concerted effort to solve it
• Most cases: Opportunity arises from recognizing problem and solving it

slides.title: Creative Destruction
content: • Theory by economist Joseph Schumpeter (20th century)
• Entrepreneurial innovation is the disruptive force that:
• In the process, it can also:
• Business processes designed to increase company efficiency
• Change in business development improves lifestyle
• Can make other activities or products outdated

slides.title: The Importance of Teamwork
content: - Taking shots even when others might have better chances
• Working together brings better results for all parties involved

slides.title: Benefits of Teamwork
content: - Teams offer different perspectives and ideas
- Studies: Diverse teams are more creative and perform better (up to 35%)
- Workload shared among members with different knowledge and skills
- Better job in shorter time than single person

slides.title: Benefits of Teamwork (Continued)
content: - People with different skills, experience, abilities
- Team that works well together raises spirit of friendship, loyalty, cooperation
- Positive environment increases morale, happiness, satisfaction
- Members build relationships based on trust and mutual respect

slides.title: Financial Requirements
content: • All businesses need money to finance different activities
- Comes from investment in share company or personal loans
- Used for: start-up costs, major developments, expansions
- Repaid when firm can afford it
- Rewarded by dividends or capital gains

slides.title: Types of Capital
content: - Used for: raw materials, covering other costs
- Requirements vary considerably by business type
- Used for: plants, machinery, equipment, company vehicles, buildings

slides.title: Sources of Finance
content: Financial resources are essential but difficult for entrepreneurial projects
- First place entrepreneurs should look for start-up money
- Should provide at least half of start-up funds
- Entrepreneur should describe opportunities and risks
- Take on partners to expand capital formation

slides.title: Sources of Finance (Continued)
content: - Expect high return and high growth potential
- Provide: start-up capital, development funds, expansion funds
• Financing is more than getting money:
